y7-2: These results do not support recommending routine supplements for everyone. However, they may not apply to people with bone disorders or those taking osteoporosis medicines; don’t stop a supplement your doctor has recommended on your own. The researchers suggest redirecting resources towards balance and strength exercise, which has been shown to prevent falls, and towards falls prevention programmes tailored to each person.
y7-3: In a systematic review published in The BMJ, Canadian researchers analysed 69 randomised trials with 153,902 adults that compared calcium, vitamin D or both with placebo or no treatment. Calcium (11 trials, 9,067 people), vitamin D (36 trials, 92,045 people) and the two combined (15 trials, 51,126 people) did not meaningfully reduce fractures, hip fractures or falls. The results were similar regardless of age, sex, previous fractures or falls and dietary calcium intake; the certainty of the evidence was mostly moderate to high.

y7-7: Standard calculators used to estimate heart risk, such as SCORE2, picked up only a small share of the people who had plaque. But this is a prevalence study: it has not yet been shown that screening everyone, or giving preventive treatment based on imaging, reduces heart attacks; a second phase to test this is planned. The finding is a reminder that blood vessel health starts in youth.
y7-8: In Denmark and Spain, 16,808 people aged 18–70 with no known cardiovascular disease had the arteries in their neck, legs and heart scanned with advanced imaging. In the REACT study, presented at the European Society of Cardiology congress on 29 August 2026 and published in the New England Journal of Medicine, 57.1% of participants had plaque in their artery walls (atherosclerosis). Between the ages of 18 and 29, 1 in 13 had plaque in at least one artery; at 60–70, the figure was about 9 in 10. In men, plaque started 5–10 years earlier than in women; in women, the steepest rise came between 40 and 60, around the menopause.

y7-13: This is a review of observational studies: it does not prove that heavy work causes dementia, and the certainty of the evidence ranges from low to very low. The researchers try to explain this ‘physical activity paradox’ with factors such as stress in physically demanding jobs, insufficient recovery, little control over one’s work, noise and air pollution. The practical takeaway: a day of tiring work may not replace movement you choose to do and recover from.
y7-14: In a review published in The Lancet Public Health, researchers from the University of Southern California in the US and from Brazil pooled data from 74 studies and more than 4.2 million people in 30 countries (median follow-up 10 years, more than 64,000 cases of dementia). Overall, the most active people had a 20% lower risk of dementia, a 21% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease and a 29% lower risk of vascular dementia. But the type of activity mattered: sport, dancing and exercise in leisure time were linked to a 24% lower risk, while people in physically demanding jobs had a 20% higher risk, rising as the work got heavier. Housework was linked to a 15% lower risk and walking or cycling to work to a 10% higher risk; these two rest on very few studies.
y7-15: Leisure-time activity lowers dementia risk; heavy physical work may raise it
